claim: Animal cell migration is predominantly driven by the coordinated, yet stochastic, polymerization of thousands of nanometer-scale actin filaments across micron-scale cell leading edges.
source: Animal cell migration is predominantly driven by the coordinated, yet stochastic, polymerization of thousands of nanometer-scale actin filaments across micron-scale cell leading edges.
evidence: This is a general statement about the mechanism of cell migration, drawing from established scientific understanding of actin-based motility.

claim: Lamellipodial stability naturally emerges from the interplay between branched actin network growth and leading edge shape with no additional feedback required.
source: Remarkably, we find lamellipodial stability naturally emerges from the interplay between branched actin network growth and leading edge shape – with no additional feedback required – based on a synergy between membrane-proximal branching and lateral spreading of filaments.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling results presented in the manuscript, specifically the findings shown in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: The Arp2/3-mediated ~70–80° branching angle optimally smooths lamellipodial shape.
source: Furthermore, our model suggests that the Arp2/3-mediated ~70–80° branching angle optimally smooths lamellipodial shape, addressing its long-mysterious conservation from protists to mammals.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 5, where different branching angles were tested.

claim: Cell migration driven by actin polymerization plays an essential role in countless organisms spanning the eukaryotic tree of life.
source: Cell migration driven by actin polymerization plays an essential role in countless organisms spanning the eukaryotic tree of life (Pollard and Cooper, 2009; Fritz-Laylin et al., 2017a; Welch et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The single actin filament polymerizes stochastically by addition of single monomers to push the leading edge membrane forward.
source: In all cases, the fundamental molecular unit of these micron-scale structures is the single actin filament, which polymerizes stochastically by addition of single monomers to push the leading edge membrane forward (Mogilner and Oster, 1996; Peskin et al., 1993; Theriot et al., 1992; Prass et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature describing the mechanism of actin polymerization.

claim: The lamellipodium is a flat 'leaf-like' protrusion that is ~200 nm tall, up to 100 µm wide, and filled with a dense network of dendritically branched actin filaments.
source: Perhaps the archetype of dynamically stable actin structures is the lamellipodium, a flat 'leaf-like' protrusion that is ~200 nm tall, up to 100 µm wide, and filled with a dense network of dendritically branched actin filaments (Svitkina et al., 1997; Abraham et al., 1999; Laurent et al., 2005; Fritz-Laylin et al., 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature describing lamellipodial structure.

claim: Cell types that undergo lamellipodial migration can maintain a single, stable lamellipodium for minutes to hours.
source: Cell types that undergo lamellipodial migration (most notably fish epidermal keratocytes and vertebrate neutrophils) can maintain a single, stable lamellipodium for minutes to hours, allowing the cells to carry out their biological functions (Tsai et al., 2019; Lacayo et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Neutrophils must undergo persistent migration over millimeter-scale distances to reach sites of inflammation and infection.
source: For example, in their in vivo role as first responders of the innate immune system, neutrophils must undergo persistent migration over millimeter-scale distances to reach sites of inflammation and infection (de Oliveira et al., 2016; Kolaczkowska and Kubes, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature describing neutrophil function.

claim: Membrane tension has been identified as a potential contributor to lamellipodial shape stability.
source: It has been widely been assumed for decades that some sort of regulatory or mechanical feedback mechanism must be required for lamellipodial shape stability, with extensive experimental efforts identifying membrane tension (Diz-Muñoz et al., 2016; Houk et al., 2012; Mueller et al., 2017; Gauthier et al., 2012; Tsujita et al., 2015; Batchelder et al., 2011; Sens and Plastino, 2015), plasma membrane curvature-sensing proteins (Tsujita et al., 2015; Pipathsouk et al., 2019), a competition for membrane-associated free monomers (Mullins et al., 2018), and force-feedback via directional filament branching (Risca et al., 2012) as potential contributors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Plasma membrane curvature-sensing proteins have been identified as potential contributors to lamellipodial shape stability.
source: It has been widely been assumed for decades that some sort of regulatory or mechanical feedback mechanism must be required for lamellipodial shape stability, with extensive experimental efforts identifying membrane tension (Diz-Muñoz et al., 2016; Houk et al., 2012; Mueller et al., 2017; Gauthier et al., 2012; Tsujita et al., 2015; Batchelder et al., 2011; Sens and Plastino, 2015), plasma membrane curvature-sensing proteins (Tsujita et al., 2015; Pipathsouk et al., 2019), a competition for membrane-associated free monomers (Mullins et al., 2018), and force-feedback via directional filament branching (Risca et al., 2012) as potential contributors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Competition for membrane-associated free monomers has been identified as a potential contributor to lamellipodial shape stability.
source: It has been widely been assumed for decades that some sort of regulatory or mechanical feedback mechanism must be required for lamellipodial shape stability, with extensive experimental efforts identifying membrane tension (Diz-Muñoz et al., 2016; Houk et al., 2012; Mueller et al., 2017; Gauthier et al., 2012; Tsujita et al., 2015; Batchelder et al., 2011; Sens and Plastino, 2015), plasma membrane curvature-sensing proteins (Tsujita et al., 2015; Pipathsouk et al., 2019), a competition for membrane-associated free monomers (Mullins et al., 2018), and force-feedback via directional filament branching (Risca et al., 2012) as potential contributors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Force-feedback via directional filament branching has been identified as a potential contributor to lamellipodial shape stability.
source: It has been widely been assumed for decades that some sort of regulatory or mechanical feedback mechanism must be required for lamellipodial shape stability, with extensive experimental efforts identifying membrane tension (Diz-Muñoz et al., 2016; Houk et al., 2012; Mueller et al., 2017; Gauthier et al., 2012; Tsujita et al., 2015; Batchelder et al., 2011; Sens and Plastino, 2015), plasma membrane curvature-sensing proteins (Tsujita et al., 2015; Pipathsouk et al., 2019), a competition for membrane-associated free monomers (Mullins et al., 2018), and force-feedback via directional filament branching (Risca et al., 2012) as potential contributors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The stability of lamellipodia has been theoretically proposed to depend on the dendritically branched structure of their actin networks.
source: The stability of lamellipodia has also been theoretically proposed to depend on the dendritically branched structure of their actin networks, wherein filaments are oriented at an angle relative to the cell's direction of migration, allowing growing filament tips to spread out laterally along the leading edge as they polymerize (Lacayo et al., 2007; Grimm et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published theoretical work.

claim: Filament orientation in cells has been experimentally observed to average ±35° relative to the membrane normal.
source: Although any acute angle would permit spreading, we note that filament orientation in cells has been experimentally observed to be highly stereotyped, averaging ±35° relative to the membrane normal (Maly and Borisy, 2001; Verkhovsky et al., 2003) – approximately one half of the highly evolutionarily-conserved ~70° branch angle mediated by the Arp2/3 complex (Mullins et al., 1998; Volkmann et al., 2001; Rouiller et al., 2008.)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published experimental measurements.

claim: The Arp2/3 complex mediates a highly evolutionarily-conserved ~70° branch angle.
source: Although any acute angle would permit spreading, we note that filament orientation in cells has been experimentally observed to be highly stereotyped, averaging ±35° relative to the membrane normal (Maly and Borisy, 2001; Verkhovsky et al., 2003) – approximately one half of the highly evolutionarily-conserved ~70° branch angle mediated by the Arp2/3 complex (Mullins et al., 1998; Volkmann et al., 2001; Rouiller et al., 2008.)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Dendritic branching is an autocatalytic process which can lead to explosive growth.
source: For instance, dendritic branching is an autocatalytic process which can lead to explosive growth (Mullins et al., 2018; Carlsson, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The growth rates of the actin network are dependent on the velocity of the flexible membrane surface it is pushing, in a manner which imparts hysteresis to the system.
source: In addition, the growth rates of the actin network are dependent on the velocity of the flexible membrane surface it is pushing, in a manner which imparts hysteresis to the system (Mueller et al., 2017; Parekh et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: High-speed imaging revealed that the leading edge shape is extremely dynamic at shorter time and length scales, constantly undergoing fine-scale fluctuations around the average cell shape.
source: In contrast to the remarkable overall lamellipodial stability observed over minutes, high-speed imaging revealed that the leading edge shape is extremely dynamic at shorter time and length scales, constantly undergoing fine-scale fluctuations around the average cell shape.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Shape fluctuations continually dissipate in a manner quantitatively consistent with viscous relaxation back to the time-averaged leading edge shape.
source: We determined that these shape fluctuations continually dissipate (thereby enabling long time scale lamellipodial maintenance) in a manner quantitatively consistent with viscous relaxation back to the time-averaged leading edge shape.
evidence: This claim is supported by the autocorrelation analysis presented in Figure 1e-h.

claim: The minimal stochastic model of branched actin network growth against a flexible membrane was able to recapitulate the global leading edge stability and fine-scale fluctuation relaxation behavior observed in cells.
source: We next developed a minimal stochastic model of branched actin network growth against a flexible membrane, broadly applicable to a wide variety of cell types, that was able to recapitulate the global leading edge stability and fine-scale fluctuation relaxation behavior observed in cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results presented in Figure 2.

claim: The suppression of stochastic fluctuations is an intrinsic, emergent property of collective actin dynamics at the leading edge.
source: Our model suggests that the suppression of stochastic fluctuations is an intrinsic, emergent property of collective actin dynamics at the leading edge, as branched network geometry alone is necessary and sufficient to generate lamellipodial stability.
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results, particularly those shown in Figure 4.

claim: Neutrophils form lamellipodia that are intrinsically lamellar, maintaining a thin, locally flat sheet of actin even in the absence of support structures like the substrate surface.
source: Neutrophils form lamellipodia that are intrinsically lamellar, maintaining a thin, locally flat sheet of actin even in the absence of support structures like the substrate surface (Fritz-Laylin et al., 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: HL-60 cells in quasi-two-dimensional confinement can migrate persistently, maintaining nearly-constant cell shape, for time scales on the order of minutes to hours.
source: Cells in this type of confinement can migrate persistently, maintaining nearly-constant cell shape, for time scales on the order of minutes to hours (Tsai et al., 2019; Garner et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: High-speed (20 Hz) imaging of migrating HL-60 cells revealed dynamic, fine-scale fluctuations around the average leading edge shape.
source: These experiments revealed dynamic, fine-scale fluctuations around the average leading edge shape (Figure 1a–c, Video 1, Figure 1—figure supplements 1–2, Materials and methods), where local instabilities in the leading edge emerge, grow, and then relax.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1a-c and Video 1.

claim: The lamellipodial dynamics observed in HL-60 cells are phenotypically distinct from and almost 100-fold faster than the oscillatory protrusion-retraction cycles seen in other, slower-moving cell types.
source: Notably, these previously-unobserved lamellipodial dynamics are phenotypically distinct from – and almost 100-fold faster than – the oscillatory protrusion-retraction cycles seen in other, slower-moving cell types (e.g. fibroblasts) (Giannone et al., 2004; Ryan et al., 2012; Ma et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with published literature on other cell types.

claim: Fluctuations with wavelengths as small as ~650 nm and amplitudes down to ~65 nm were reliably measured.
source: We estimate we were able to reliably measure fluctuations with wavelengths as small as ~650 nm, and amplitudes down to ~65 nm, by fitting the phase contrast halo around the leading edge (Figure 1—figure supplements 1–2, Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by the segmentation methods described in the Materials and methods section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 1–2.

claim: The measured wavelengths and amplitudes should approximately correspond to 25 actin filaments at physiological spacing and 25 actin monomers assembled into a filament lattice along the direction of motion.
source: These values should approximately correspond to 25 actin filaments at physiological spacing (Svitkina et al., 1997) and 25 actin monomers assembled into a filament lattice along the direction of motion.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the measured values and known physiological parameters from the literature.

claim: Kymograph analysis of curvature and velocity showed that relatively long-lived shape fluctuations are formed by the continual time-integration of seemingly uncorrelated and very short-lived velocity fluctuations.
source: In particular, kymograph analysis of curvature and velocity (Figure 1b–c) showed that relatively long-lived shape fluctuations are formed by the continual time-integration of seemingly uncorrelated and very short-lived (sub-second, sub-micron) velocity fluctuations.
evidence: This claim is supported by the kymograph analysis shown in Figure 1b-c.

claim: Autocorrelation analysis revealed a monotonic relaxation of shape fluctuations at each wavelength.
source: Autocorrelation analysis revealed a monotonic relaxation of shape fluctuations at each wavelength (Figure 1e–f); the decay at every spatial scale is well-fit by an exponential form (Figure 1f), consistent with overdamped viscous relaxation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the autocorrelation analysis shown in Figure 1e-f.

claim: The decay at every spatial scale is well-fit by an exponential form, consistent with overdamped viscous relaxation.
source: Autocorrelation analysis revealed a monotonic relaxation of shape fluctuations at each wavelength (Figure 1e–f); the decay at every spatial scale is well-fit by an exponential form (Figure 1f), consistent with overdamped viscous relaxation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the fitting results shown in Figure 1f.

claim: No increase in the autocorrelation over time was detected, which would have appeared if there were any sustained, correlated growth of the fluctuations before they decay.
source: Importantly, we do not detect any increase in the autocorrelation over time, which would have appeared if there were any sustained, correlated growth of the fluctuations before they decay.
evidence: This claim is supported by the autocorrelation analysis results shown in Figure 1.

claim: A clear wavelength-dependence is observed, with shorter wavelengths decaying faster and having smaller amplitudes.
source: A clear wavelength-dependence is observed, with shorter wavelengths decaying faster and having smaller amplitudes (Figure 1g–h).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1g-h.

claim: The qualitative and quantitative properties of the leading edge fluctuations are not specific to cell type or experimental conditions, as they are also observed in fish epidermal keratocytes.
source: Importantly, these qualitative and quantitative properties of the leading edge fluctuations are not specific to cell type or experimental conditions (e.g. agarose overlay, ECM), as we also observe this phenomenon in fish epidermal keratocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 6, Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6 and Video 2.

claim: The model incorporated a two-dimensional leading edge with filaments polymerizing against a flexible membrane, modeled as a system of flat membrane segments coupled elastically to each other.
source: Expanding on this general framework, and in an approach conceptually similar to previous work simulating small (< 2 µm) patches of a lamellipodium (Schaus et al., 2007; Schaus and Borisy, 2008), we incorporated a two-dimensional leading edge with filaments polymerizing against a flexible membrane, which we modeled as a system of flat membrane segments coupled elastically to each other.
evidence: This is a description of the computational model developed in this work.

claim: Simulated filaments apply force to the membrane following the classic untethered Brownian ratchet formalism.
source: Simulated filaments apply force to the membrane following the classic untethered Brownian ratchet formalism (Mogilner and Oster, 1996), consistent with recent experiments showing that cellular protrusions are formed by largely untethered actin networks (Bisaria et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim describes a feature of the model and is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The model incorporated experimentally measured values from the literature for the membrane tension, membrane bending modulus, and biochemical rate constants.
source: Designed to be as comparable as possible to our experimental data, the model incorporated experimentally measured values from the literature for the membrane tension, membrane bending modulus, and biochemical rate constants (Tables 1–2, Mogilner and Oster, 1996; Lieber et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim describes the parameterization of the model using literature values.

claim: The model included only the core biochemical elements of actin network growth dynamics: polymerization, depolymerization, branching, and capping.
source: As we were specifically interested in identifying biophysical mechanisms regulating leading edge stability, we minimized the model's biological complexity by including only the core biochemical elements of actin network growth dynamics: polymerization, depolymerization, branching, and capping.
evidence: This claim describes the design choices made in developing the model.

claim: All filament nucleation in the model occurs through dendritic branching mediated by the Arp2/3 complex.
source: All filament nucleation in the model occurs through dendritic branching observed in cells to be mediated by the Arp2/3 complex (Welch et al., 1997; Svitkina et al., 1997), which catalyzes the nucleation of new 'daughter' actin filaments as branches from the sides of pre-existing 'mother' filaments at a characteristic angle of ~70° (Mullins et al., 1998; Volkmann et al., 2001; Rouiller et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim describes a feature of the model and is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The Arp2/3 complex catalyzes the nucleation of new 'daughter' actin filaments as branches from the sides of pre-existing 'mother' filaments at a characteristic angle of ~70°.
source: All filament nucleation in the model occurs through dendritic branching observed in cells to be mediated by the Arp2/3 complex (Welch et al., 1997; Svitkina et al., 1997), which catalyzes the nucleation of new 'daughter' actin filaments as branches from the sides of pre-existing 'mother' filaments at a characteristic angle of ~70° (Mullins et al., 1998; Volkmann et al., 2001; Rouiller et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The minimal model was able to recapitulate stable leading edge fluctuations.
source: To our great surprise, this very simple model was able to recapitulate stable leading edge fluctuations.
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results presented in Figure 2.

claim: Nascent leading edges reach steady state values for filament density, filament length, filament angle, membrane velocity, and membrane fluctuation amplitude within seconds.
source: Nascent leading edges reach steady state values for filament density, filament length, filament angle, membrane velocity, and (most importantly) membrane fluctuation amplitude within seconds, a biologically realistic time scale (Figure 2d–h).
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2d-h.

claim: The steady state values obtained from the model are in quantitative agreement with both experimental data and previously published measurements.
source: Furthermore, the steady state values obtained are in quantitative agreement with both our own experimental data and previously published measurements, with the model yielding mean values of: 0.3 filaments/nm for filament density (~30 nm filament spacing for a lamellipodium that is 10 filaments tall) (Abraham et al., 1999), ~150 nm for filament length, ~40° for filament angle (with respect to the direction of migration), ~0.35 nm/ms for membrane velocity, and ~50 nm for membrane fluctuation amplitude (Svitkina et al., 1997; Maly and Borisy, 2001; Verkhovsky et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results with experimental data and literature values.

claim: Simulated leading edge shape stability is mediated by an exponential decay of shape fluctuations.
source: As observed in the experimental measurements, simulated leading edge shape stability is mediated by an exponential decay of shape fluctuations (Figure 2i–j).
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2i-j.

claim: The minimal model correctly predicts the monotonic trends of fluctuation amplitude and decay time scale with wavelength.
source: Furthermore, the minimal model correctly predicts the monotonic trends of fluctuation amplitude and decay time scale with wavelength (Figure 2k–l) in a way that was not sensitive to our choices of simulation time step, membrane segment length, and overall length of the leading edge (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2k-l and the control simulations shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3.

claim: The simulated fluctuation relaxation behavior emerges directly from the molecular-scale actin growth model, with all biochemical parameters estimated from measurements in the existing literature.
source: It should be noted that the generation of the simulated data in Figure 2k–l did not involve any curve-fitting (and therefore no free parameters that could be fit) to the experimentally measured autocorrelation dynamics in order to parameterize the model. Rather, the simulated fluctuation relaxation behavior, qualitatively reproducing our experimental measurements, emerges directly from the molecular-scale actin growth model, in which all biochemical parameters were estimated from measurements in the existing literature (Tables 1–2) – leaving no free simulation parameters.
evidence: This claim describes the parameterization approach used in the model.

claim: Cells treated with Latrunculin B present with enhanced bleb formation and more variable leading edge shapes, in comparison with cells treated with a DMSO vehicle control.
source: Qualitatively, cells treated with Latrunculin B (Video 4) present with enhanced bleb formation and more variable leading edge shapes, in comparison with cells treated with a DMSO vehicle control (Video 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental observations shown in Videos 4 and 5.

claim: At low effective doses of Latrunculin B, the model predicts an increase in the amplitudes at large wavelengths and a decrease in the decay rates across all wavelengths.
source: At low effective doses, subtle but measurable changes to leading edge fluctuations were predicted: specifically, an increase in the amplitudes at large wavelengths, and a decrease in the decay rates across all wavelengths (Figure 3a–b).
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 3a-b.

claim: Experimental results with Latrunculin B-treated cells were consistent with the quantitative predictions from the model.
source: Our experimental results were consistent with these quantitative predictions; Latrunculin B-treated cells exhibited increased fluctuation amplitudes and decreased fluctuation rates over the predicted ranges (Figure 3c–d).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3c-d.

claim: The coupling between the membrane segments (i.e. the effects of tension and bending at length scales larger than the size of an individual membrane segment) was completely dispensable for leading edge stability.
source: Surprisingly, the coupling between the membrane segments (i.e. the effects of tension and bending at length scales larger than the size of an individual membrane segment) was completely dispensable for leading edge stability (Figure 4a–e).
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 4a-e.

claim: Only two elements were required for stability: constraining branching to occur only within a fixed distance from the leading edge membrane, and the ability of filaments to spread laterally to neighboring membrane segments.
source: Following a similar process of elimination, we determined that in fact only two elements were required for stability. First, as reported previously for dendritic actin network polymerization against a single stiff obstacle, it was necessary to constrain branching to occur only within a fixed distance from the leading edge membrane (Figure 2a–b) in order to maintain a steady state actin density (Carlsson, 2001). The molecular motivation for this spatially limited 'branching window' is rooted in that fact that activators of the Arp2/3 complex, which render Arp2/3 competent for actin filament nucleation, are typically membrane-associated proteins (Suetsugu, 2013). Second, we found that stability is inherently tied to the ability of filaments to spread laterally to neighboring membrane segments (Figure 2b II-III, Figure 4f–i).
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: Removing filament spreading from the model led to actin density divergence: network regions with low filament density eventually underwent complete depolymerization, while high-density regions continued to accumulate actin.
source: Removing filament spreading from the model by fixing filaments to remain associated with their nearest membrane segment at birth (Materials and methods) led to actin density divergence: network regions with low filament density eventually underwent complete depolymerization, while high-density regions continued to accumulate actin (Figure 4f–g).
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 4f-g.

claim: Leading edge maintenance is an intrinsic, emergent property of branched actin network growth against a membrane, without requiring any further regulatory governance.
source: Remarkably, this means that leading edge maintenance is an intrinsic, emergent property of branched actin network growth against a membrane, without requiring any further regulatory governance.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the simulation results showing that only branching and spreading are required for stability.

claim: Geometrical constraints imposed simply by the nature of membrane-proximal actin branching ensure that any small variations in either local actin filament density or growth rate are inherently self-correcting to regress toward the mean.
source: Geometrical constraints imposed simply by the nature of membrane-proximal actin branching ensure that any small variations in either local actin filament density or growth rate are inherently self-correcting to regress toward the mean.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the simulation results and the proposed molecular mechanism shown in Figure 4j.

claim: Arp2/3-mediated branching is required for lamellipodial formation in a wide variety of cell types.
source: Of note, it has previously been shown that Arp2/3-mediated branching is required for lamellipodial formation in a wide variety of cell types; cells with inhibited or depleted Arp2/3 complex exhibit complete disruption of the lamellipodium shape and often switch to a different mode of migration altogether, such as filopodial motility (Fritz-Laylin et al., 2017b; Henson et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2012; Davidson et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: HL-60s treated with the Arp2/3 inhibitor CK-666 have extremely variable leading edge shapes, characterized by long, thin filopodia-like protrusions.
source: Indeed, HL-60s treated with the Arp2/3 inhibitor CK-666 have extremely variable leading edge shapes, characterized by long, thin filopodia-like protrusions (Video 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental observations shown in Video 6.

claim: The vital lamellipodial maintenance role of Arp2/3-mediated branching stems from its ability to mediate efficient filament spreading and equilibration of actin density fluctuations.
source: Our theoretical results provide a mechanistic interpretation for this striking phenomenon, suggesting that the vital lamellipodial maintenance role of Arp2/3-mediated branching stems from its ability to mediate efficient filament spreading and equilibration of actin density fluctuations, purely because the daughter filament always grows at an angle distinct from its mother.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the simulation results.

claim: When filaments are initialized with a random orientation and the branching angle is fixed, only a handful of the initial filament angles survive until the end of the simulation.
source: For example, when filaments are initialized with a random orientation, and the branching angle is fixed (i.e. there is no variability in the branching angle), only a handful of the initial filament angles (θf) survive until the end of the simulation (Figure 5a).
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The surviving, successful filament angles are narrowly and symmetrically distributed around one half of the branching angle.
source: The surviving, successful filament angles are narrowly and symmetrically distributed around one half of the branching angle (Figure 5a–c).
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 5a-c.

claim: The Arp2/3 complex is highly conserved.
source: Intriguingly, this protein complex is highly conserved (Welch et al., 1997), with measurements of the branching angle in a wide variety of species, including protists (Mullins et al., 1998; Volkmann et al., 2001; Rouiller et al., 2008; Blanchoin et al., 2000), yeast (Rouiller et al., 2008), mammals (Rouiller et al., 2008; Blanchoin et al., 2000; Cai et al., 2008), and amphibians (Svitkina and Borisy, 1999), using various experimental techniques (platinum replica electron microscopy, cryo-electron microscopy, and total internal reflection microscopy), all falling within the range of 67–78° (± 2–13°).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Measurements of the branching angle in a wide variety of species all fall within the range of 67–78° (± 2–13°).
source: Intriguingly, this protein complex is highly conserved (Welch et al., 1997), with measurements of the branching angle in a wide variety of species, including protists (Mullins et al., 1998; Volkmann et al., 2001; Rouiller et al., 2008; Blanchoin et al., 2000), yeast (Rouiller et al., 2008), mammals (Rouiller et al., 2008; Blanchoin et al., 2000; Cai et al., 2008), and amphibians (Svitkina and Borisy, 1999), using various experimental techniques (platinum replica electron microscopy, cryo-electron microscopy, and total internal reflection microscopy), all falling within the range of 67–78° (± 2–13°).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In simulations with no branch angle variability, a 70–80° branching angle was optimal for minimizing both actin density fluctuations and leading edge fluctuation amplitudes for wavelengths smaller than ~2 µm.
source: Excitingly, we found that in simulations with no branch angle variability, a 70–80° branching angle was optimal for minimizing both actin density fluctuations (Figure 5d and i) and leading edge fluctuation amplitudes for wavelengths smaller than ~2 µm (Figure 5f and h).
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 5d, f, h, and i.

claim: The smoothing effects of the optimal branching angle are predicted to be relevant within the experimentally-measurable range of wavelengths (between ~0.7 µm and ~2 µm), but are most beneficial for the smallest wavelengths resolved by the simulations (down to ~0.3 µm).
source: These smoothing effects are therefore predicted to be relevant within the experimentally-measurable range of wavelengths (between ~0.7 µm and ~2 µm), but are most beneficial for the smallest wavelengths resolved by our simulations (down to ~0.3 µm) – closest to the length scales of individual filament polymerization.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the simulation results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Decreasing orientational heritability significantly reduces the dependence of fluctuation amplitude and filament density variability on the branching angle.
source: Perhaps unsurprisingly, decreasing this orientational heritability significantly reduces the dependence of fluctuation amplitude and filament density variability on the branching angle (Figure 5j–q), and thereby counteracts the beneficial effect of the optimal angle on leading edge fluctuations.
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 5j-q.

claim: Introducing a branch angle variability of ±2° broadens the range of near-optimal branch angles but maintains the optimum at ~70–80°.
source: Introducing a branch angle variability of ±2° (on the lower end of the experimentally-measured values) broadens the range of near-optimal branch angles but maintains the optimum at ~70–80° (Figure 5j and l), while introducing a variability of ±10° (on the higher end of the measured range) completely removes the optimum (Figure 5n and p).
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 5j, l, n, and p.

claim: Introducing a branch angle variability of ±10° completely removes the optimum.
source: Introducing a branch angle variability of ±2° (on the lower end of the experimentally-measured values) broadens the range of near-optimal branch angles but maintains the optimum at ~70–80° (Figure 5j and l), while introducing a variability of ±10° (on the higher end of the measured range) completely removes the optimum (Figure 5n and p).
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 5n and p.

claim: Increasing the branch angle variability increases the minimum possible fluctuation amplitude and filament density variability, representing a decrease in the noise-suppression capabilities of the system.
source: In both cases, increasing the branch angle variability increases the minimum possible fluctuation amplitude (Figure 5h, l and p – insets) and filament density variability (Figure 5i, m and q), representing a decrease in the noise-suppression capabilities of the system.
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 5h, i, l, m, p, and q.

claim: Actin network geometry is not only essential for leading edge stability, but also plays a major role in determining the fundamental limits of smoothness in lamellipodial shape.
source: Overall, these results provide strong support for the idea that actin network geometry is not only essential for leading edge stability, but also plays a major role in determining the fundamental limits of smoothness in lamellipodial shape.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the simulation results shown in Figure 5.

claim: The suppression of stochastic fluctuations naturally emerges from the interactions between a growing actin network and the leading edge membrane, with no additional feedback required.
source: In this work, application of that principle in combination with high-precision measurements, quantitative analytical techniques, and physical modeling led to the surprising revelation that the suppression of stochastic fluctuations naturally emerges from the interactions between a growing actin network and the leading edge membrane, with no additional feedback required.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main finding of the manuscript, supported by the experimental and computational results.

claim: The model provides an understanding of the basic biophysical mechanisms underlying lamellipodial migration.
source: The model developed in this work provides an understanding of the basic biophysical mechanisms underlying lamellipodial migration.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Lateral filament spreading, combined with a fixed branching window, is indispensable for leading edge stability.
source: By selectively removing elements of the model, we determined that lateral filament spreading, combined with a fixed branching window, is indispensable for leading edge stability.
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 4.

claim: A ~70–80° branch angle maximally suppresses fine-scale actin density and leading edge shape fluctuations.
source: Our further investigations into the evolutionary properties of actin network growth revealed that a ~70–80° branch angle maximally suppresses fine-scale actin density and leading edge shape fluctuations, showing for the first time that Arp2/3-mediated branching imparts optimal functionality, as was long hypothesized based on strong sequence, structural, and functional conservation throughout the eukaryotic tree of life.
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 5.

claim: The evolutionarily-conserved branching angle that maximally suppresses leading edge fluctuations appears not to be the same angle that optimizes the polymerization velocity of single filaments.
source: It is interesting to note that the evolutionarily-conserved branching angle that we find maximally suppresses leading edge fluctuations appears not to be the same angle that optimizes the polymerization velocity of single filaments – predicted to be a broad angle closer to ~90–100° (and quite load-dependent) in the low-load regime (Mogilner and Oster, 1996).
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from comparison of the simulation results with published theoretical predictions.

claim: Evolutionary selection acts at the level of actin network properties, rather than force production by individual filaments.
source: This contrast suggests that evolutionary selection acts at the level of actin network properties, rather than force production by individual filaments.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the comparison between optimal angles for different properties.

claim: Stability in the case of lamellipodial dynamics is inherently encoded by the geometry of branched actin network growth.
source: Returning to the broader question of how noisy biological systems control for stochasticity, we find that stability in the case of lamellipodial dynamics is inherently encoded by the geometry of branched actin network growth.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the modeling results.
